1	Gaming PC vs. Console: Which Should You Buy in 2024?
     2	 Ease of Use
     3	 Let’s get the most obvious point out of the way: a game console is much, much easier to use than a
     4	gaming PC.
     5	 Modern game consoles are a bit more complex than their predecessors, and users do need to know a
     6	bit about HDR, resolution, and refresh rate for the best experience. But PC gamers need to know all
     7	that, and more. Drivers, BIOS updates, hardware compatibility, software conflicts, Windows
     8	Updates...the list goes on.
     9	 A PC also requires more patience when installing and launching a game. Launching a game on Xbox,
    10	PlayStation 5, or Switch usually takes mere seconds. The Xbox Series X|S and PlayStation 5 even have
    11	“quick resume” features that let you pick up precisely where you left off without reloading the game
    12	(so long as you haven’t played another in the meantime).
    13	 This is an easy win for consoles. They provide the quickest, simplest path to launching and playing
    14	a game. Though some handheld gaming PCs do a decent job as well.
    15	 Winner: Console
    16	 Affordability
    17	 Affordability is another clear win for consoles. It’s possible to buy a gaming PC for the price of
    18	an Xbox Series X or PlayStation 5, but you’ll end up with an outdated graphics card that can’t
    19	handle games designed for modern game consoles.
    20	 Gamers that can’t quite afford the Xbox Series X or Playstation 5 will find fine alternatives in
    21	the Xbox Series S and Nintendo Switch. PCs sold at prices comparable to entry-level consoles, on the
    22	other hand, usually lack a graphics card. They’ll struggle even in games that are five years old, or
    23	older.
    24	 Affordable PC gaming is possible. Handheld gaming PCs like the Steam Deck and AMD Ryzen-based
    25	mini-PCs like the Beelink SER6 MAX are surprisingly capable for their size and price. Still, they’re
    26	best when playing indie games with 2D graphics or cross-platform titles from the Xbox One /
    27	PlayStation 4 era (or older)—and they’re certainly not comparable to a Xbox Series X|S or
    28	PlayStation 5.
    29	 Winner: Console
    30	 Overall Value
    31	 Game consoles are less expensive than a gaming PC, but that doesn’t mean they’re a better value. A
    32	console is built to handle specific tasks—gaming and media streaming. A PC is as much a tool as an
    33	entertainment device and can be used for everything from web browsing to video editing and software
    34	development.
    35	 That’s relevant. Many people who own a game console will also want a computer, so it’s not fair to
    36	compare the total cost of a gaming PC against the price of a game console. It’s more sensible to
    37	compare the extra cash you paid to purchase a gaming PC (instead of a more barebones computer)
    38	against the price of the game console.
    39	 PC gamers looking for a good mid-range, off-the-shelf desktop or gaming laptop with performance
    40	comparable to an Xbox Series X or PlayStation 5 will need to spend $1,500 to $2,000 (depending on
    41	whether you’re fine with an basic desktop from Dell or HP, or want something from a boutique like
    42	Origin PC or Digital Storm). DIY gamers can build a console-slaying desktop for under $1,500 with an
    43	AMD Ryzen 5600X processor and a solid budget GPU, like a Radeon RX 7800 XT graphics card.
    44	 That’s still a lot of money. But if you need a solid PC for other demanding tasks, you’ll need to
    45	budget around $1,000 to buy it, which makes the price difference between the PC and console less
    46	extreme.
    47	 And while new gaming PCs are expensive, many popular PC games aren’t demanding and don’t require
    48	expensive hardware. Games like Counter-Strike 2, DOTA 2, Team Fortress 2, Grand Theft Auto V, War
    49	Thunder, and Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Siege regularly top Steam’s charts. All of these games are
    50	playable even on PCs with an ancient video card like the Nvidia GTX 1060 or AMD Radeon RX 570.
    51	 Winner: Tie
    52	 Game Library Differences
    53	 The game library available to modern game consoles is remarkable. Most games are now
    54	cross-platform, so the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and Nintendo Switch share many titles. The
    55	PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S are backwards-compatible with many previous-gen titles, too, which
    56	boosts the game library of each console into the thousands.
    57	 Compared to a gaming PC, however, those numbers look absolutely adorable.
    58	 The game library available to a modern gaming PC is a mystery, because there’s too many to count.
    59	An estimate of over 100,000 titles is safe: over 12,000 games were released to Steam in 2022 alone.
    60	A PC can also emulate the game library of most older titles and, in some cases, even modern games—a
    61	PC is arguably the best way to enjoy The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, if you can get it
    62	working (and buy a copy of the game, as emulating the game without buying it is piracy).
    63	 A PC is the way to go if you want access to the largest game library on the face of the planet.
    64	 Winner: PC
    65	 Performance and Visuals
    66	 In June of 2019 I found a chair in Los Angeles' Peacock Theater and let Microsoft’s Xbox press
    67	conference wash over me. It was an exciting year, as hype was brewing for Sony and Microsoft’s
    68	respective next-gen consoles. And that hype included a now long-forgotten promise: 8K resolution at
    69	up to 120 frames per second.
    70	 It wasn’t exactly a lie: the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X can technically output a 8K signal,
    71	and also output 120 frames per second. But it was marketing bullshit. The most graphically demanding
    72	games are lucky to upscale to 4K at a framerate of 60 FPS, with many titles including a 30 FPS
    73	“graphics” or “visuals” mode.
    74	 PC gaming is a different world. 60 FPS is considered the bare minimum for an optimal experience,
    75	and a framerate of 120 FPS or greater is preferable. 8K gaming isn’t really a thing even on the PC
    76	(though technically possible, I suppose, if you have a rare 8K television), but a native resolution
    77	beyond at and beyond 4K is possible. The Samsung Neo G9 57-inch super-ultrawide, which supports a
    78	native resolution of 7,680 x 2,160, is arguably the most extreme gaming display available right
    79	now—and gaming at its native resolution is only possible on a PC.
    80	 Console titles also tend to use a lower quality preset than what’s available on PC. The details
    81	vary from game to game, with some better optimized than others. Generally speaking, however, most
    82	games available on the PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X|S have visuals similar to the “Medium” or
    83	“High” preset in the PC release.
    84	 Ray-tracing is another win for the PC. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S can handle ray-tracing
    85	(a feature heavily marketed in the run-up to their release), but game support is underwhelming. Even
    86	some big “next-gen” exclusives, like Starfield, fail to include it. Cross-platform titles that
    87	support ray-tracing, like Cyberpunk 2077, usually stick to a level of quality that’s a notch or two
    88	below the maximum available on PC.
    89	 It’s not all good news for the PC. Nvidia’s habit of stiffing gamers on video memory is catching up
    90	to cards with less than 16GB of video memory—the amount supported by the PlayStation 5 and Xbox
    91	Series X. Optimization problems can also cause problems in some PC ports. And, of course, achieving
    92	the best possible PC gaming experience can prove extremely expensive.
    93	 Still, the fact remains that PC gaming beats console gaming on both performance (as measured by
    94	framerate) and visual quality. This gap will only increase in the coming years as the current

Based solely on `doc.txt` ("Gaming PC vs. Console: Which Should You Buy in 2024?"), here's how the two compare on your three points:

**1. Raw graphical performance (PC wins)**
- The current console generation (PS5, Xbox Series X|S) can technically output 8K and 120 FPS, but the document calls that "marketing bullshit." In practice, the most graphically demanding games are "lucky to upscale to 4K at a framerate of 60 FPS," and many titles include a 30 FPS "graphics" or "visuals" mode.
- On PC, 60 FPS is considered the bare minimum, 120+ FPS is preferable, and native resolutions beyond 4K are possible (e.g., 7,680 x 2,160 on the Samsung Neo G9 super-ultrawide — playable only on PC).
- Console versions of games generally run on lower quality presets — roughly equivalent to the "Medium" or "High" preset of the PC release.
- **Ray tracing:** a win for PC. Consoles can handle it, but game support is "underwhelming" — even big next-gen exclusives like Starfield lack it. Cross-platform titles that do support it, like Cyberpunk 2077, "usually stick to a level of quality that's a notch or two below the maximum available on PC."
- Caveats for PC: Nvidia's tendency to under-provide video memory is catching up to cards with less than 16GB of VRAM (the amount PS5 and Xbox Series X have), and some PC ports have optimization problems. The document concludes PC beats console on both framerate and visual quality, and that gap will widen as this console generation ages.

**2. Game availability (PC wins)**
- Consoles have a "remarkable" library: most games are cross-platform, and backwards compatibility with previous-gen titles boosts each console's library into the thousands.
- But compared to PC, "those numbers look absolutely adorable." A PC's library is estimated at over 100,000 titles — over 12,000 games were released on Steam in 2022 alone. A PC can also emulate most older game libraries and, in some cases, even modern games.

**3. Price of a solid PC that keeps up with consoles**
- A good mid-range, off-the-shelf desktop or gaming laptop with performance comparable to an Xbox Series X or PS5: **$1,500–$2,000** (basic Dell/HP desktops at the lower end; boutique builders like Origin PC or Digital Storm at the higher end).
- DIY route: a "console-slaying" desktop for **under $1,500** with an AMD Ryzen 5600X and a budget GPU like a Radeon RX 7800 XT.
- Warning: a PC priced like an Xbox Series X or PS5 will have an outdated graphics card that can't handle games designed for modern consoles, and PCs at entry-level console prices usually lack a proper GPU entirely.

**Bottom line for your use case:** Since you want Cyberpunk-level visuals with ray tracing and high FPS, the document's evidence points to PC — consoles cap out around upscaled 4K/60 FPS (often 30 FPS in graphics mode) and run ray tracing a notch or two below PC quality, while a $1,500–$2,000 PC (or a sub-$1,500 DIY build) is what it takes to match or beat the current consoles.
